Alternatively, an authorization may be granted in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004, read in conjunction with Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006 [2]. 

Furthermore, any medicinal product appearing in the Annex cannot be placed on the market within the Community unless a marketing authorization has been granted by the Community in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 [3]. 

The authorization requirement also applies to radionuclide generators, radionuclide kits, radionuclide precursor radiopharmaceuticals, and industrially prepared radiopharmaceuticals [1].
reference: A marketing authorisation. No medicinal product may be placed on the market of a Member State unless a marketing authorisation has been issued by that Member State's competent authorities under the Directive, or an authorisation has been granted at Union level under the centralised procedure.

user_input: What are the rules for clinical trials on medicinal products?
retrieved_contexts:
['Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on clinical trials on medicinal products for human use, and repealing Directive 2001/20/EC Text with EEA relevance | CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS | Article 3 General principle
A clinical trial may be conducted only if:
(a) the rights, safety, dignity and well-being of subjects are protected and prevail over all other interests; and
(b) it is designed to generate reliable and robust data.', 'Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on clinical trials on medicinal products for human use, and repealing Directive 2001/20/EC Text with EEA relevance | CHAPTER V PROTECTION OF SUBJECTS AND INFORMED CONSENT | Article 28 General rules
1. A clinical trial may be conducted only where all of the following conditions are met:
(a) the anticipated benefits to the subjects or to public health justify the foreseeable risks and inconveniences and compliance with this condition is constantly monitored;
(b) the subjects, or where a subject is not able to give informed consent, his or her legally designated representative, have been informed in accordance with Article 29(2) to (6);
(c) the subjects, or where a subject is not able to give informed consent, his or her legally designated representative, have given informed consent in accordance with Article 29(1), (7) and (8);
(d) the rights of the subjects to physical and mental integrity, to privacy and to the protection of the data concerning them in accordance with Directive 95/46/EC are safeguarded;
(e) the clinical trial has been designed to involve as little pain, discomfort, fear and any other foreseeable risk as possible for the subjects and both the risk threshold and the degree of distress are specifically defined in the protocol and constantly monitored;
(f) the medical care provided to the subjects is the responsibility of an appropriately qualified medical doctor or, where appropriate, a qualified dental practitioner;
(g) the subject or, where the subject is not able to give informed consent, his or her legally designated representative has been provided with the contact details of an entity where further information can be received in case of need;
(h) no undue influence, including that of a financial nature, is exerted on subjects to participate in the clinical trial.', 'Directive 2001/83/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 November 2001 on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use | Annex I ANALYTICAL, PHARMACOTOXICOLOGICAL AND CLINICAL STANDARDS AND PROTOCOLS IN RESPECT OF THE TESTING OF MEDICINAL PRODUCTS
1. In general, clinical trials shall be done as "controlled clinical trials" and if possible, randomized; any other design shall be justified. The treatment of the control groups will vary from case to case and also will depend on ethical considerations; thus it may, in some instances, be more pertinent to compare the efficacy of a new medicinal product with that of an established medicinal product of proven therapeutic value rather than with the effect of a placebo.
As far as possible, and particularly in trials where the effect of the product cannot be objectively measured, steps shall be taken to avoid bias, including methods of randomization and blinding.
2. The protocol of the trial must include a thorough description of the statistical methods to be employed, the number and reasons for inclusion of patients (including calculations of the power of the trial), the level of significance to be used and a description of the statistical unit. Measures taken to avoid bias, particularly methods of randomization, shall be documented. Inclusion of a large number of subjects in a trial must not be regarded as an adequate substitute for a properly controlled trial.
3. Clinical statements concerning the efficacy or safety of a medicinal product under normal conditions of use which are not scientifically substantiated cannot be accepted as valid evidence.
4. The value of data on the efficacy and safety of a medicinal product under normal conditions of use will be very greatly enhanced if such data come from several competent investigators working independently.
5. For vaccines and serums, the immunological status and age of the trial population and the local epidemiology are of critical importance and shall be monitored during the trial and fully described.
For live attenuated vaccines, clinical trials shall be so designed as to reveal potential transmission of the immunizing agent from vaccinated to non-vaccinated subjects. If transmission is possible, the genotypic and phenotypic stability of the immunizing agent shall be studied.
For vaccines and allergen products, follow-up studies shall include appropriate immunological tests, and where applicable, antibody assays.', "Directive 2001/83/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 November 2001 on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use | Annex I ANALYTICAL, PHARMACOTOXICOLOGICAL AND CLINICAL STANDARDS AND PROTOCOLS IN RESPECT OF THE TESTING OF MEDICINAL PRODUCTS
A clinical trial is any systematic study of medicinal products in human subjects whether in patients or non-patient volunteers in order to discover or verify the effects of and/or identify any adverse reaction to investigational products, and/or study their absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion in order to ascertain the efficacy and safety of the products.
Evaluation of the application for marketing authorization shall be based on clinical trials including clinical pharmacological trials designed to determine the efficacy and safety of the product under normal conditions of use, having regard to the therapeutic indications for use in human beings. Therapeutic advantages must outweigh potential risks.
A. General requirements
The clinical particulars to be provided pursuant to Articles 8(3)(i) and 10(1) must enable a sufficiently well-founded and scientifically valid opinion to be formed as to whether the medicinal product satisfies the criteria governing the granting of a marketing authorization. Consequently, an essential requirement is that the results of all clinical trials should be communicated, both favourable and unfavourable.
Clinical trials must always be preceded by adequate pharmacological and toxicological tests, carried out on animals in accordance with the requirements of Part 3 of this Annex. The investigator must acquaint himself with the conclusions drawn from the pharmacological and toxicological studies and hence the applicant must provide him at least with the investigator's brochure, consisting of all the relevant information known prior to the onset of a clinical trial including chemical, pharmaceutical and biological data, toxicological, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data in animals and the results of earlier clinical trials, with adequate data to justify the nature, scale and duration of the proposed trial; the complete pharmacological and toxicological reports shall be provided on request. For materials of human or animal origin, all available means shall be employed to ensure safety from transmission of infectious agents prior to the commencement of the trial.
B. Conduct of trials
1. Good clinical practice", 'Commission Directive 2003/63/EC of 25 June 2003 amending Directive 2001/83/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use (Text with EEA relevance) | Annex
In general, clinical trials shall be done as "controlled clinical trials" if possible, randomised and as appropriate versus placebo and versus an established medicinal product of proven therapeutic value; any other design shall be justified. The treatment of the control groups will vary from case to case and also will depend on ethical considerations and therapeutic area; thus it may, in some instances, be more pertinent to compare the efficacy of a new medicinal product with that of an established medicinal product of proven therapeutic value rather than with the effect of a placebo.
(1) As far as possible, and particularly in trials where the effect of the product cannot be objectively measured, steps shall be taken to avoid bias, including methods of randomisation and blinding.
(2) The protocol of the trial must include a thorough description of the statistical methods to be employed, the number and reasons for inclusion of patients (including calculations of the power of the trial), the level of significance to be used and a description of the statistical unit. Measures taken to avoid bias, particularly methods of randomisation, shall be documented. Inclusion of a large number of subjects in a trial must not be regarded as an adequate substitute for a properly controlled trial.
The safety data shall be reviewed taking into account guidelines published by the Commission, with particular attention to events resulting in changes of dose or need for concomitant medication, serious adverse events, events resulting in withdrawal, and deaths. Any patients or patient groups at increased risk shall be identified and particular attention paid to potentially vulnerable patients who may be present in small numbers, e.g., children, pregnant women, frail elderly, people with marked abnormalities of metabolism or excretion etc. The implication of the safety evaluation for the possible uses of the medicinal product shall be described.
5.2.5.2. Study reports of uncontrolled clinical studies reports of analyses of data from more than one study and other clinical study reports
These reports shall be provided.
5.2.6. Reports of post-marketing experience', "Directive 2001/83/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 November 2001 on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use | Annex I ANALYTICAL, PHARMACOTOXICOLOGICAL AND CLINICAL STANDARDS AND PROTOCOLS IN RESPECT OF THE TESTING OF MEDICINAL PRODUCTS
1.1. All phases of clinical investigation, including bioavailability and bioequivalence studies, shall be designed, implemented and reported in accordance with good clinical practice.
1.2. All clinical trials shall be carried out in accordance with the ethical principles laid down in the current revision of the Declaration of Helsinki. In principle, the freely given informed consent of each trial subject shall be obtained and documented.
The trial protocol (including statistical design), the technical application and documentation shall be submitted by the sponsor and/or investigator for an opinion to the relevant ethics committee. The trials shall not begin before the opinion of this committee has been received in writing.
1.3. Pre-established, systematic written procedures for the organization, conduct, data collection, documentation and verification of clinical trials shall be required.
1.4. In the case of radiopharmaceuticals, clinical trials shall be carried out under the responsibility of a medical doctor authorized to use radionuclides for medical purposes.
2. Archiving
The marketing authorization holder shall make arrangements for archiving of documentation.
(a) The investigator shall arrange for the retention of the patient identification codes for at least 15 years after the completion or discontinuation of the trial.
(b) Patient files and other source data shall be kept for the maximum period of time permitted by the hospital, institution or private practice.
(c) The sponsor or other owner of the data shall retain all other documentation pertaining to the trial as long as the product is authorized. These procedures shall include:
- the protocol including the rationale, objectives and statistical design and methodology of the trial, with conditions under which it is performed and managed, and details of the investigational product, the reference medicinal product and/or the placebo used,
- standard operating procedures,
- all written opinions on the protocol and procedures,
- the investigator's brochure,
- case report forms on each trial subject,
- final report,
- audit certificate(s), if available."]
response:
Based on the provided sources, the rules for clinical trials on medicinal products include:

* **General Principles:** Clinical trials may only be conducted if the rights, safety, dignity, and well-being of subjects are protected and prevail over all other interests, and if the trial is designed to generate reliable and robust data [1]. 
* **Conditions for Conduct:** Anticipated benefits to subjects or public health must justify foreseeable risks and inconveniences, and this must be constantly monitored [2]. Trials must involve as little pain, discomfort, fear, and foreseeable risk as possible, with risk thresholds and distress degrees specifically defined in the protocol and constantly monitored [2]. Furthermore, no undue financial or other influence may be exerted on subjects [2], and medical care must be the responsibility of an appropriately qualified medical doctor or dental practitioner [2].
* **Informed Consent and Rights:** Subjects (or their legally designated representatives if unable to consent) must be properly informed and have given informed consent [2][6]. Rights to physical and mental integrity, privacy, and data protection must be safeguarded [2], and subjects must receive contact details for an entity providing further information [2]. Trials must also follow the ethical principles of the current revision of the Declaration of Helsinki [6].
* **Design and Methodology:** Clinical trials must be preceded by adequate pharmacological and toxicological animal tests [4]. In general, trials should be "controlled clinical trials", randomized, and—as appropriate—versus placebo and an established medicinal product of proven therapeutic value, with any other design requiring justification [3][5]. Steps must be taken to avoid bias (such as randomization and blinding) [3][5], and protocols must thoroughly describe statistical methods, power calculations, significance levels, and the number and reasons for including patients [3][5]. 
* **Administrative and Procedural Rules:** Trials must be designed, implemented, and reported in accordance with good clinical practice [6]. The protocol, technical application, and documentation must be submitted to the relevant ethics committee, and trials cannot begin until a written opinion is received [6]. Comprehensive records, data, and documentation must be retained and archived by investigators, hospitals, sponsors, or marketing authorization holders according to specified retention periods [6].
reference: A clinical trial may be conducted only if the rights, safety, dignity and well-being of subjects are protected and prevail over all other interests and it is designed to generate reliable and robust data. It needs prior authorisation after scientific and ethical review, and subjects, or their legally designated representatives, must be informed and give informed consent; the anticipated benefits must justify the foreseeable risks.

user_input: How are medical devices classified by risk?
retrieved_contexts:
["Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on medical devices, amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and repealing Council Directives 90/385/EEC and... | ANNEX VIII CLASSIFICATION RULES
— if they are intended to allow direct diagnosis or monitoring of vital physiological processes, unless they are specifically intended for monitoring of vital physiological parameters and the nature of variations of those parameters is such that it could result in immediate danger to the patient, for instance variations in cardiac performance, respiration, activity of the central nervous system, or they are intended for diagnosis in clinical situations where the patient is in immediate danger, in which cases they are classified as class IIb.
Active devices intended to emit ionizing radiation and intended for diagnostic or therapeutic radiology, including interventional radiology devices and devices which control or monitor such devices, or which directly influence their performance, are classified as class IIb.
6.3. Rule 11
Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is classified as class IIa, except if such decisions have an impact that may cause:
— death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health, in which case it is in class III; or
— a serious deterioration of a person's state of health or a surgical intervention, in which case it is classified as class IIb.
Software intended to monitor physiological processes is classified as class IIa, except if it is intended for monitoring of vital physiological parameters, where the nature of variations of those parameters is such that it could result in immediate danger to the patient, in which case it is classified as class IIb.
All other software is classified as class I.
6.4. Rule 12
All active devices intended to administer and/or remove medicinal products, body liquids or other substances to or from the body are classified as class IIa, unless this is done in a manner that is potentially hazardous, taking account of the nature of the substances involved, of the part of the body concerned and of the mode of application in which case they are classified as class IIb.
6.5. Rule 13
All other active devices are classified as class I.
7. SPECIAL RULES", 'Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on medical devices, amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and repealing Council Directives 90/385/EEC and... | CHAPTER V CLASSIFICATION AND CONFORMITY ASSESSMENT | SECTION 1 Classification | Article 51 Classification of devices
1. Devices shall be divided into classes I, IIa, IIb and III, taking into account the intended purpose of the devices and their inherent risks. Classification shall be carried out in accordance with Annex VIII.
2. Any dispute between the manufacturer and the notified body concerned, arising from the application of Annex VIII, shall be referred for a decision to the competent authority of the Member State in which the manufacturer has its registered place of business. In cases where the manufacturer has no registered place of business in the Union and has not yet designated an authorised representative, the matter shall be referred to the competent authority of the Member State in which the authorised representative referred to in the last indent of point (b) of the second paragraph of Section 2.2 of Annex IX has its registered place of business. Where the notified body concerned is established in a Member State other than that of the manufacturer, the competent authority shall adopt its decision after consultation with the competent authority of the Member State that designated the notified body.
The competent authority of the Member State in which the manufacturer has its registered place of business shall notify the MDCG and the Commission of its decision. The decision shall be made available upon request.
3. At the request of a Member State the Commission shall after consulting the MDCG, decide, by means of implementing acts, on the following:
(a) application of Annex VIII to a given device, or category or group of devices, with a view to determining the classification of such devices;
(b) that a device, or category or group of devices, shall for reasons of public health based on new scientific evidence, or based on any information which becomes available in the course of the vigilance and market surveillance activities be reclassified, by way of derogation from Annex VIII.', 'Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on medical devices, amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and repealing Council Directives 90/385/EEC and... | ANNEX VIII CLASSIFICATION RULES
— are intended specifically to control, diagnose, monitor or correct a defect of the heart or of the central circulatory system through direct contact with those parts of the body, in which case they are classified as class III;
— are intended specifically for use in direct contact with the heart or central circulatory system or the central nervous system, in which case they are classified as class III;
— are intended to supply energy in the form of ionizing radiation in which case they are classified as class IIb;
— have a biological effect or are wholly or mainly absorbed in which case they are classified as class III;
— are intended to undergo chemical change in the body in which case they are classified as class IIb, except if the devices are placed in the teeth; or
— are intended to administer medicines, in which case they are classified as class IIb.
5.4. Rule 8
All implantable devices and long-term surgically invasive devices are classified as class IIb unless they:
— are intended to be placed in the teeth, in which case they are classified as class IIa;
— are intended to be used in direct contact with the heart, the central circulatory system or the central nervous system, in which case they are classified as class III;
— have a biological effect or are wholly or mainly absorbed, in which case they are classified as class III;
— are intended to undergo chemical change in the body in which case they are classified as class III, except if the devices are placed in the teeth;
— are intended to administer medicinal products, in which case they are classified as class III;
— are active implantable devices or their accessories, in which cases they are classified as class III;
— are breast implants or surgical meshes, in which cases they are classified as class III;', 'Regulation (EU) 2017/746 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices and repealing Directive 98/79/EC and Commission Decision 2010/227/EU (Text with EEA relevance. ) | CHAPTER V CLASSIFICATION AND CONFORMITY ASSESSMENT | Section 1 Classification | Article 47 Classification of devices
1. Devices shall be divided into classes A, B, C and D, taking into account the intended purpose of the devices and their inherent risks. Classification shall be carried out in accordance with Annex VIII.
2. Any dispute between the manufacturer and the notified body concerned, arising from the application of Annex VIII, shall be referred for a decision to the competent authority of the Member State in which the manufacturer has its registered place of business. In cases where the manufacturer has no registered place of business in the Union and has not yet designated an authorised representative, the matter shall be referred to the competent authority of the Member State in which the authorised representative referred to in the last indent of point (b) of the second paragraph of Section 2.2. of Annex IX has its registered place of business. Where the notified body concerned is established in a Member State other than that of the manufacturer, the competent authority shall adopt its decision after consultation with the competent authority of the Member State that designated the notified body.
The competent authority of the Member State in which the manufacturer has its registered place of business shall notify the MDCG and the Commission of its decision. The decision shall be made available upon request.
3. At the request of a Member State, the Commission shall after consulting the MDCG, decide, by means of implementing acts, on the following:
(a) application of Annex VIII to a given device, or category or group of devices, with a view to determining the classification of such devices;
(b) that a device, or category or group of devices, shall for reasons of public health based on new scientific evidence, or based on any information which becomes available in the course of the vigilance and market surveillance activities be reclassified, by way of derogation from Annex VIII.
4. The Commission may also, on its own initiative and after consulting the MDCG, decide, by means of implementing acts, on the issues referred to in points (a) and (b) of paragraph 3.', 'Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on medical devices, amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and repealing Council Directives 90/385/EEC and... | Recitals (58)
(58) It is necessary, in particular for the purpose of the conformity assessment procedures, to maintain the division of devices into four product classes in line with international practice. The classification rules, which are based on the vulnerability of the human body, should take into account the potential risks associated with the technical design and manufacture of the devices. To maintain the same level of safety as provided by Directive 90/385/EEC, active implantable devices should be in the highest risk class.', 'Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2017 on medical devices, amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and repealing Council Directives 90/385/EEC and... | ANNEX VIII CLASSIFICATION RULES
All devices incorporating or consisting of nanomaterial are classified as:
— class III if they present a high or medium potential for internal exposure;
— class IIb if they present a low potential for internal exposure; and
— class IIa if they present a negligible potential for internal exposure.
7.7. Rule 20
All invasive devices with respect to body orifices, other than surgically invasive devices, which are intended to administer medicinal products by inhalation are classified as class IIa, unless their mode of action has an essential impact on the efficacy and safety of the administered medicinal product or they are intended to treat life-threatening conditions, in which case they are classified as class IIb.
7.8. Rule 21
Devices that are composed of substances or of combinations of substances that are intended to be introduced into the human body via a body orifice or applied to the skin and that are absorbed by or locally dispersed in the human body are classified as:
— class III if they, or their products of metabolism, are systemically absorbed by the human body in order to achieve the intended purpose;
— class III if they achieve their intended purpose in the stomach or lower gastrointestinal tract and they, or their products of metabolism, are systemically absorbed by the human body;
— class IIa if they are applied to the skin or if they are applied in the nasal or oral cavity as far as the pharynx, and achieve their intended purpose on those cavities; and
— class IIb in all other cases.
7.9. Rule 22
Active therapeutic devices with an integrated or incorporated diagnostic function which significantly determines the patient management by the device, such as closed loop systems or automated external defibrillators, are classified as class III.']
response: Medical devices are divided into four product classes—I, IIa, IIb, and III—taking into account their intended purpose, inherent risks, the vulnerability of the human body, and potential risks associated with their technical design and manufacture [2][5].
reference: Devices are divided into classes I, IIa, IIb and III, taking into account their intended purpose and inherent risks, with classification carried out according to the rules in Annex VIII. Disputes between the manufacturer and the notified body are decided by the competent authority.

user_input: What rules apply to the cross-border healthcare of patients?
retrieved_contexts:
['Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare | Recitals (19)
(19) When a patient receives cross-border healthcare, it is essential for the patient to know in advance which rules will be applicable. The rules applicable to cross-border healthcare should be those set out in the legislation of the Member State of treatment, given that, in accordance with Article 168(7) TFEU, the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care is the responsibility of the Member States. This should help the patient in making an informed choice, and should avoid misapprehension and misunderstanding. It should also establish a high level of trust between the patient and the healthcare provider.', 'Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare | CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS | Article 1 Subject matter and scope
1. This Directive provides rules for facilitating the access to safe and high-quality cross-border healthcare and promotes cooperation on healthcare between Member States, in full respect of national competencies in organising and delivering healthcare. This Directive also aims at clarifying its relationship with the existing framework on the coordination of social security systems, Regulation (EC) No 883/2004, with a view to application of patients’ rights.
2. This Directive shall apply to the provision of healthcare to patients, regardless of how it is organised, delivered and financed.
3. This Directive shall not apply to:
(a) services in the field of long-term care the purpose of which is to support people in need of assistance in carrying out routine, everyday tasks;
(b) allocation of and access to organs for the purpose of organ transplants;
(c) with the exception of Chapter IV, public vaccination programmes against infectious diseases which are exclusively aimed at protecting the health of the population on the territory of a Member State and which are subject to specific planning and implementation measures.
4. This Directive shall not affect laws and regulations in Member States relating to the organisation and financing of healthcare in situations not related to cross-border healthcare. In particular, nothing in this Directive obliges a Member State to reimburse costs of healthcare provided by healthcare providers established on its own territory if those providers are not part of the social security system or public health system of that Member State.', 'Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare | CHAPTER II RESPONSIBILITIES OF MEMBER STATES WITH REGARD TO CROSS-BORDER HEALTH CARE | Article 4 Responsibilities of the Member State of treatment
1. Taking into account the principles of universality, access to good quality care, equity and solidarity, cross-border healthcare shall be provided in accordance with:
(a) the legislation of the Member State of treatment;
(b) standards and guidelines on quality and safety laid down by the Member State of treatment; and
(c) Union legislation on safety standards.', 'Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare | CHAPTER II RESPONSIBILITIES OF MEMBER STATES WITH REGARD TO CROSS-BORDER HEALTH CARE | Article 4 Responsibilities of the Member State of treatment
3. The principle of non-discrimination with regard to nationality shall be applied to patients from other Member States.
This shall be without prejudice to the possibility for the Member State of treatment, where it is justified by overriding reasons of general interest, such as planning requirements relating to the aim of ensuring sufficient and permanent access to a balanced range of high-quality treatment in the Member State concerned or to the wish to control costs and avoid, as far as possible, any waste of financial, technical and human resources, to adopt measures regarding access to treatment aimed at fulfilling its fundamental responsibility to ensure sufficient and permanent access to healthcare within its territory. Such measures shall be limited to what is necessary and proportionate and may not constitute a means of arbitrary discrimination and shall be made publicly available in advance.
4. Member States shall ensure that the healthcare providers on their territory apply the same scale of fees for healthcare for patients from other Member States, as for domestic patients in a comparable medical situation, or that they charge a price calculated according to objective, non-discriminatory criteria if there is no comparable price for domestic patients.
This paragraph shall be without prejudice to national legislation which allows healthcare providers to set their own prices, provided that they do not discriminate against patients from other Member States.
5. This Directive shall not affect laws and regulations in Member States on the use of languages. Member States may choose to deliver information in other languages than those which are official languages in the Member State concerned.', 'Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare | CHAPTER III REIMBURSEMENT OF COSTS OF CROSS-BORDER HEALTHCARE | Article 7 General principles for reimbursement of costs
4. The costs of cross-border healthcare shall be reimbursed or paid directly by the Member State of affiliation up to the level of costs that would have been assumed by the Member State of affiliation, had this healthcare been provided in its territory without exceeding the actual costs of healthcare received.
Where the full cost of cross-border healthcare exceeds the level of costs that would have been assumed had the healthcare been provided in its territory the Member State of affiliation may nevertheless decide to reimburse the full cost.
The Member State of affiliation may decide to reimburse other related costs, such as accommodation and travel costs, or extra costs which persons with disabilities might incur due to one or more disabilities when receiving cross-border healthcare, in accordance with national legislation and on the condition that there be sufficient documentation setting out these costs.
5. Member States may adopt provisions in accordance with the TFEU aimed at ensuring that patients enjoy the same rights when receiving cross-border healthcare as they would have enjoyed if they had received healthcare in a comparable situation in the Member State of affiliation.
6. For the purposes of paragraph 4, Member States shall have a transparent mechanism for calculation of costs of cross-border healthcare that are to be reimbursed to the insured person by the Member State of affiliation. This mechanism shall be based on objective, non-discriminatory criteria known in advance and applied at the relevant (local, regional or national) administrative level.', 'Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare | CHAPTER III REIMBURSEMENT OF COSTS OF CROSS-BORDER HEALTHCARE | Article 7 General principles for reimbursement of costs
7. The Member State of affiliation may impose on an insured person seeking reimbursement of the costs of cross-border healthcare, including healthcare received through means of telemedicine, the same conditions, criteria of eligibility and regulatory and administrative formalities, whether set at a local, regional or national level, as it would impose if this healthcare were provided in its territory. This may include an assessment by a health professional or healthcare administrator providing services for the statutory social security system or national health system of the Member State of affiliation, such as the general practitioner or primary care practitioner with whom the patient is registered, if this is necessary for determining the individual patient’s entitlement to healthcare. However, no conditions, criteria of eligibility and regulatory and administrative formalities imposed according to this paragraph may be discriminatory or constitute an obstacle to the free movement of patients, services or goods, unless it is objectively justified by planning requirements relating to the object of ensuring sufficient and permanent access to a balanced range of high-quality treatment in the Member State concerned or to the wish to control costs and avoid, as far as possible, any waste of financial, technical and human resources.
8. The Member State of affiliation shall not make the reimbursement of costs of cross-border healthcare subject to prior authorisation except in the cases set out in Article 8.
9. The Member State of affiliation may limit the application of the rules on reimbursement for cross-border healthcare based on overriding reasons of general interest, such as planning requirements relating to the aim of ensuring sufficient and permanent access to a balanced range of high-quality treatment in the Member State concerned or to the wish to control costs and avoid, as far as possible, any waste of financial, technical and human resources.
10. Notwithstanding paragraph 9, Member States shall ensure that the cross-border healthcare for which a prior authorisation has been granted is reimbursed in accordance with the authorisation.']
response:
When a patient receives cross-border healthcare, the rules applicable are those set out in the legislation of the Member State of treatment [1]. Furthermore, cross-border healthcare must be provided in accordance with:
- the legislation of the Member State of treatment [3];
- standards and guidelines on quality and safety laid down by the Member State of treatment [3]; and
- Union legislation on safety standards [3].
reference: The Member State of affiliation must reimburse the costs of cross-border healthcare if the treatment is among the benefits the patient is entitled to at home. Costs are reimbursed up to the level that would have been paid had the care been provided at home, without exceeding the actual cost; the Member State may choose to reimburse more, such as travel and accommodation.

Article 4 Eligibility of donors: Blood establishments shall ensure that donors of whole blood and blood components comply with the eligibility criteria set out in Annex III.
Article 5 Storage, transport and distribution conditions for blood and blood components: Blood establishments shall ensure that the storage, transport and distribution conditions for blood and blood components comply with the requirements set out in Annex IV.
Article 6 Quality and safety requirements for blood and blood components: Blood establishments shall ensure that the quality and safety requirements for blood and blood components comply with the requirements set out in Annex V.', 'Directive 2002/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 January 2003 setting standards of quality and safety for the collection, testing, processing, storage and distribution of human blood and blood components and amending... | CHAPTER VI PROVISIONS FOR THE QUALITY AND SAFETY OF BLOOD AND BLOOD COMPONENTS | Article 21 Testing of donations
Blood establishments shall ensure that each donation of blood and blood components is tested in conformity with requirements listed in Annex IV.
Member States shall ensure that blood and blood components imported into the Community are tested in conformity with requirements listed in Annex IV.
Article 22 Storage, transport and distribution conditions: Blood establishments shall ensure that the storage, transport and distribution conditions of blood and blood components comply with the requirements referred to in Article 29(e).
Article 23 Quality and safety requirements for blood and blood components: Blood establishments shall ensure that quality and safety requirements for blood and blood components meet the high standards in compliance with the requirements referred to in Article 29(f).', 'Directive 2002/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 January 2003 setting standards of quality and safety for the collection, testing, processing, storage and distribution of human blood and blood components and amending... | Annex Iii LABELLING REQUIREMENTS
The label on the component must contain the following information:
- the official name of the component
- the volume or weight or number of cells in the component (as appropriate)
- the unique numeric or alphanumeric donation identification
- the name of producing blood establishment
- the ABO Group (not required for plasma intended only for fractionation)
- the Rh D Group, either Rh D positive or Rh D negative (not required for plasma intended only for fractionation)
- the date or time of expiry (as appropriate)
- the temperature of storage
- the name, composition and volume of anticoagulant and/or additive solution (if any).', 'Directive 2002/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 January 2003 setting standards of quality and safety for the collection, testing, processing, storage and distribution of human blood and blood components and amending... | Annex Iv BASIC TESTING REQUIREMENTS FOR WHOLE BLOOD AND PLASMA DONATIONS
The following tests must be performed for whole blood and apheresis donations, including autologous predeposit donations:
- ABO Group (not required for plasma intended only for fractionation)
- Rh D Group (not required for plasma intended only for fractionation)
- testing for the following infections in the donors:
- Hepatitis B (HBs-Ag)
- Hepatitis C (Anti-HCV)
- HIV 1/2 (Anti-HIV 1/2)
Additional tests may be required for specific components or donors or epidemiological situations.', 'Commission Directive 2004/33/EC of 22 March 2004 implementing Directive 2002/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards certain technical requirements for blood and blood components (Text with EEA relevance) | Annex Iv STORAGE, TRANSPORT AND DISTRIBUTION CONDITIONS FOR BLOOD AND BLOOD COMPONENTS
(as referred to in Article 5)
1. STORAGE
1.1. Liquid storage
>TABLE>
1.2. Cryopreservation
>TABLE>
2. TRANSPORT AND DISTRIBUTION
Transport and distribution of blood and blood components at all stages of the transfusion chain must be under conditions that maintain the integrity of the product.
3. ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR AUTOLOGOUS DONATIONS
3.1. Autologous blood and blood components must be clearly identified as such and stored, transported and distributed separately from allogeneic blood and blood components.
3.2. Autologous blood and blood components must be labelled as required by Directive 2002/98/EC and in addition the label must include the identification of the donor and the warning "FOR AUTOLOGOUS TRANSFUSION ONLY".']
response:
Based on the provided sources, blood and blood components are subject to several requirements:

* **Quality and Safety Requirements:** Blood establishments must ensure that quality and safety requirements comply with the standards set out in Annex V of Directive 2004/33/EC [1][2], meeting high standards in compliance with Article 29(f) of Directive 2002/98/EC [3]. This includes complying with technical quality measurements, meeting acceptable results, performing appropriate bacteriological control of the collection and manufacturing process, and ensuring imports from third countries meet equivalent standards [1]. 
* **Testing:** Each donation of blood and blood components must be tested in conformity with the requirements listed in Annex IV of Directive 2002/98/EC, which applies to both blood establishments and imports into the Community [3][5].
* **Storage, Transport, and Distribution:** Storage, transport, and distribution conditions must comply with the requirements referred to in Article 29(e) of Directive 2002/98/EC [3] and Annex IV of Directive 2004/33/EC [2], maintaining product integrity at all stages of the transfusion chain [6].
* **Labelling:** Components must include specific information on their label, such as the official name, volume/weight/cell count, unique donation identification, producing blood establishment, ABO and Rh D groups (with exceptions for plasma intended only for fractionation), expiry date/time, storage temperature, and details of any anticoagulant or additive solution [4].
reference: Collection and testing of blood and blood components, and their preparation, storage and distribution for transfusion, may be carried out only by blood establishments designated, authorised, accredited or licensed by the competent authority. Each donation must be tested according to Annex IV, including imported blood, and storage, transport, distribution and quality and safety must meet the required high standards.

user_input: What information must appear on food labels?
response:
Based on the provided sources, the mandatory food information that must be indicated on food labels includes:

* The name of the food [1]
* The list of ingredients [1]
* Any ingredient or processing aid listed in Annex II (or derived from a substance/product listed in Annex II) that causes allergies or intolerances and is still present in the finished product, even in an altered form [1]
* The quantity of certain ingredients or categories of ingredients [1]
* The net quantity of the food [1]
* The date of minimum durability or the ‘use by’ date [1]
* Any special storage conditions and/or conditions of use [1]
* The name or business name and address of the food business operator [1]
* The country of origin or place of provenance where applicable [1]
* Instructions for use, if necessary for appropriate use of the food [1]
* The actual alcoholic strength by volume for beverages containing more than 1,2% by volume of alcohol [1]
* A nutrition declaration [1]

The particulars must be indicated with words and numbers, and may additionally be expressed by pictograms or symbols [1]. For prepacked foods, this information must appear directly on the package or on an attached label [5], and must meet specific font size and legibility requirements [3].
reference: Mandatory particulars include the name of the food, the list of ingredients, allergens, the quantity of certain ingredients, the net quantity, the date of minimum durability or 'use by' date, special storage conditions or conditions of use, the name or business name and address of the food business operator, the country of origin where required, instructions for use where needed, the alcohol strength for drinks above 1.2% and a nutrition declaration.

user_input: What rules apply to novel foods?
response:
Based on the provided sources, the rules that apply to novel foods include the following:

* **Union List Authorisation:** Only novel foods that are authorised and included in the Union list may be placed on the market within the Union, or used in or on foods, in accordance with their specified conditions of use and labelling requirements [4]. 
* **General Conditions for Authorisation:** The Commission will only authorise a novel food and include it in the Union list if it meets specific conditions: 
  * It does not pose a safety risk to human health based on available scientific evidence [1].
  * Its intended use does not mislead the consumer (especially when replacing another food with a significant change in nutritional value) [1].
  * When intended to replace another food, its normal consumption is not nutritionally disadvantageous compared to that food [1]. 
  * If safety cannot be assessed and scientific uncertainty persists, the precautionary principle may be applied [2].
* **Authorisation Procedures:** Novel foods are authorised and the Union list is updated through specific procedures initiated either by the Commission or via an application [3][6]. Applications must include applicant details, food description, production processes, composition, scientific evidence on human health safety, analysis methods where appropriate, and proposed conditions of use or labelling requirements [6].

user_input: What direct payments can farmers receive under the common agricultural policy?
response:
Under the common agricultural policy, types of intervention in the form of direct payments may take the form of decoupled and coupled direct payments [1]. 

**Decoupled direct payments include:**
- The basic income support for sustainability [1] (which Member States provide as an annual decoupled payment per eligible hectare to active farmers) [6]. Member States may also grant a payment to small farmers as a lump sum or amounts per hectare replacing certain direct payments, with an annual payment not exceeding EUR 1 250 [2].
- The complementary redistributive income support for sustainability [1].
- The complementary income support for young farmers [1].
- The schemes for the climate, the environment and animal welfare [1].

**Coupled direct payments include:**
- Coupled income support [1] (an annual payment per hectare or animal granted to active farmers to help specific supported sectors, productions, or types of farming address difficulties) [3].
- The crop-specific payment for cotton [1].
reference: Decoupled direct payments: basic income support for sustainability, complementary redistributive income support, complementary income support for young farmers, and schemes for the climate, the environment and animal welfare (eco-schemes). Coupled direct payments: coupled income support and the crop-specific payment for cotton.

user_input: How is organic production defined and labelled?
response:
Organic production means the use of production methods compliant with EU rules at all stages of production, preparation, and distribution [2][5]. Under Regulation (EU) 2018/848, this includes use during the conversion period [5]. 

Regarding labelling, a product is considered to bear terms referring to organic production when its labelling, advertising, or commercial documents describe it, its ingredients, or feed materials in terms suggesting they were produced in accordance with the regulation [1]. Specific terms such as 'bio' and 'eco' (and their derivatives/diminutives) may be used for compliant products, but cannot be used for products that do not comply, nor can any misleading terms or practices be used [1]. Products produced during the conversion period generally cannot be labelled as organic, with exceptions for certain plant and feed products that comply with Article 10(4) and use the term "in-conversion" [1]. Additionally, these terms cannot be used for products that Union law requires to be labelled as containing, consisting of, or being produced from GMOs [1].
reference: A product bears terms referring to organic production where its labelling, advertising or commercial documents describe it, its ingredients or its feed materials in terms suggesting they were produced in accordance with the Regulation. Such terms, including 'bio' and 'eco', may only be used for products that comply with the organic production rules.

user_input: What are the rules on protected designations of origin for wine?
response:
Based on the provided sources, the rules concerning protected designations of origin for wine include:

* **Authorization to use:** A protected designation of origin may be used by any operator marketing a wine produced in conformity with the corresponding product specification [1].
* **Scope of protection:** Protected designations of origin are protected against direct or indirect commercial use by comparable products not complying with the specification or uses exploiting their reputation; misuse, imitation, or evocation (even if the true origin is indicated or translated/transliterated); false or misleading indications regarding provenance, origin, nature, or essential qualities; and any other practice liable to mislead consumers as to the true origin [1]. 
* **Generic status:** They cannot become generic in the Union [1].
* **Eligibility and production:** Traditionally used names may constitute a designation of origin if they designate a wine, refer to a geographical name, meet specific requirements, and undergo the protection procedure [3]. Production covers all operations from grape harvesting to the completion of wine-making, excluding post-production processes [3]. Additionally, applications for protection require a product specification containing elements such as analytical and organoleptic characteristics, oenological practices, geographical demarcation, yields, grape varieties, and verification bodies [4].
reference: A designation of origin is the name of a region or specific place used for a wine whose quality and characteristics are essentially or exclusively due to that geographical environment, made exclusively from grapes from that area, produced there and obtained from Vitis vinifera. A geographical indication requires a quality or reputation attributable to the origin, at least 85% of grapes from that area and production there.

user_input: What does my dog need to travel with me into the EU from another country?
response:
When moving a pet dog into the EU from a third country or territory, the dog must generally be accompanied by an animal health certificate, valid for a total of six months from the date of the checks at the entry point or until the anti-rabies vaccination expires, whichever comes first [1]. 

Alternatively, dogs may be accompanied by a passport under specific conditions [4]. Additionally, the dog must:
- Enter through a designated travellers’ point of entry, unless it originates from certain listed third countries or territories or is moved by military, law enforcement, or search-and-rescue personnel under a specific permit [5].
- Be individually identified [2].
- Have the certificate issued or endorsed by an official or authorised veterinarian not more than 10 days prior to the date of entry into the Union (extended for travel by sea) [2].
reference: The dog must be identified by an injectable transponder (microchip), show no signs of disease, have a valid anti-rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and have a valid rabies antibody titration test unless it comes from a listed country exempted from it. Dogs going to areas free of Echinococcus multilocularis need a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before entry. It must enter through a travellers' point of entry, unless coming from a listed country, and be accompanied by an animal health certificate.

user_input: What are the welfare rules for animals during transport?
response:
The welfare rules for animals during transport include the following general and technical requirements:

* **General Conditions:** Animals must not be transported in a way likely to cause injury or undue suffering [1]. Necessary arrangements must be made in advance to minimise journey length and meet the animals' needs, and animals must be fit for the journey [1]. Means of transport and loading/unload facilities must be designed, constructed, maintained, and operated to avoid injury and suffering and ensure safety [1]. Personnel must be trained or competent, carrying out tasks without violence or unnecessary fear, injury, or suffering [1]. Transport must occur without delay to the destination, and animal welfare conditions must be regularly checked and maintained [1]. Sufficient floor area and height, appropriate to size and journey, must be provided [1], and water, feed, and rest must be offered at suitable intervals appropriate to species and size [1].
* **Fitness for Transport:** No animal may be transported unless it is fit for the intended journey under guaranteed conditions that prevent injury or unnecessary suffering [2]. Specific categories of animals are deemed unfit (e.g., those unable to move independently without pain, those with severe open wounds or prolapses, heavily pregnant females, new-born mammals with unhealed navels, and certain young animals below specified age thresholds unless transported under 100 km) [2]. Exceptions are made for slightly injured or ill animals if transport causes no additional suffering, research animals under Directive 86/609/EEC, and animals transported under veterinary supervision [2]. Animals falling ill or injured during transport must be separated, receive first-aid and appropriate veterinary treatment, and undergo emergency slaughter or killing if necessary without unnecessary suffering [2].
* **Handling Rules:** Animals must be handled calmly and gently to minimise unrest, agitation, pain, distress, and injury [6]. Noise, harassment, excessive force, striking, pressure on sensitive body parts, crushing/twisting/breaking tails, grasping eyes, punching, kicking, and suspension or dragging by sensitive parts are prohibited [6]. Electric shocks must be avoided as much as possible, used only on adult bovine animals and adult pigs refusing to move when they have room ahead, applied solely to hindquarter muscles for no longer than one second, and not used repeatedly [6]. Prods or pointed implements are forbidden, and guiding sticks must be applied without causing injury or suffering [6].
reference: No one may transport animals in a way likely to cause injury or undue suffering. Journeys must be planned to minimise their length and meet the animals' needs, the animals must be fit for the journey, and the means of transport must be designed and operated to avoid injury and suffering, with competent handlers, water, feed and rest at suitable intervals.

user_input: What measures apply to control African swine fever?
response:
To eliminate outbreaks of African swine fever, measures include:
- The immediate killing or slaughter and destruction of all pigs on holdings where a clinical case is diagnosed or which are considered contaminated from an epizootiological investigation, done so as to avoid spreading the virus [1][2].
- Cleansing and disinfection of holdings, along with the elimination of insect and rodent pests [1][2].
- Immediate and adequate compensation for owners of slaughtered pigs [1][2].
- A health delay before restocking (at least one month for enclosed premises and at least three months for other holdings) [1][2].
- Gradual restocking using "sentinel" pigs checked for the absence of African swine fever antibodies [1][2].
- Continuous serological surveillance of holdings until fully restocked [1][2].
- The establishment of a protection zone with a radius of at least three kilometres for at least 30 days when a clinical case is diagnosed, with restrictions on the movement of swine [1].

Additional measures include creating regions free of African swine fever [3], preventive and restocking measures in Sardinia [4], special disease control measures set out in Regulation (EU) 2023/594 [5], and national/regional protection measures such as controlling waste and swill and banning or strictly regulating the use of pigmeat scraps for feeding [6].
reference: Special disease control measures apply in the Member States concerned, with restricted zones I, II and III and infected zones listed in the annexes. They restrict the movement of kept pigs from those zones and of germinal products, products of animal origin, animal by-products and fresh meat and meat products obtained from them, in addition to the general measures in protection, surveillance and infected zones.

The transmitted data typically includes:

* The most recent geographical position (latitude and longitude), with a specified position error margin (less than 500 metres under a 99% confidence interval in general EU rules, NAFO, NEAFC, and ICCAT areas, or less than 100 metres under normal conditions in the SPRFMO area) [1][2][3][5][6].
* The date and time (UTC) of the position fix [1][2][3][5].
* The vessel's course/heading and speed [1][2][3][5].

Additionally, Member States ensure their FMCs receive and record these positions [1][2], and that the devices are protected against input or output of false positions and cannot be manually overridden [3].
reference: Member States operate vessel monitoring systems that track the position and movement of fishing vessels flying their flag and vessels in their waters. Originally vessels of 12 metres or more had to carry a satellite tracking device; since the 2023 revision every Union fishing vessel must have a tracking device that automatically transmits its position at regular intervals and can be polled by the fisheries monitoring centre, with vessels under 12 metres allowed to use a device that is not installed on board.

response:
Under Regulation (EU) 2017/2403, specific rules govern fishing operations by Union fishing vessels in third-country waters depending on the framework:

* **Under an SFPA:** Flag Member States may only issue fishing authorisations if eligibility criteria are fulfilled, conditions of the relevant SFPA are complied with, all fees and related financial sanctions have been paid by the operator, and the vessel has a valid fishing authorisation from the third country [2]. 
* **Under agreements on exchange of fishing opportunities or joint management:** Articles 8 to 11 apply *mutatis mutandis*, with a derogation allowing flag Member States to provide vessel details to the Commission to be forwarded to the third country, after which approved vessels are considered to have a valid fishing authorisation [3].

Fishing operations cannot commence until the third country actually issues the valid authorisation [1].
reference: Union vessels need a fishing authorisation from their flag Member State to fish outside Union waters. It may only be issued if complete and accurate information on the vessel is provided, the vessel has a valid fishing licence, applies the IMO identification scheme where required, is not on an IUU vessel list, and fishing opportunities are available under the relevant fisheries agreement.

This Directive establishes a scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Community scheme’) in order to promote reductions of greenhouse gas emissions in a cost-effective and economically efficient manner.', 'Directive (EU) 2023/959 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 amending Directive 2003/87/EC establishing a system for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Union and Decision (EU) 2015/1814 concerning the... | Recitals
additional sectors’). The new system is accompanied by complementary policies shaping expectations of market participants and aiming for a carbon price signal for the whole economy while providing measures to avoid undue price impacts. Previous experience has shown that the development of the new system requires setting up an efficient monitoring, reporting and verification system. With a view to ensuring synergies and consistency with the existing Union infrastructure for the EU ETS, it is appropriate to set up an emissions trading system for the buildings, road transport and additional sectors via an amendment to Directive

1. Member States shall ensure that allowances can be transferred between:
(a) persons within the Community;
(b) persons within the Community and persons in third countries, where such allowances are recognised in accordance with the procedure referred to in Article 25 without restrictions other than those contained in, or adopted pursuant to, this Directive.
2. Member States shall ensure that allowances issued by a competent authority of another Member State are recognised for the purpose of meeting an operator's obligations under paragraph 3.
3. Member States shall ensure that, by 30 April each year at the latest, the operator of each installation surrenders a number of allowances equal to the total emissions from that installation during the preceding calendar year as verified in accordance with Article 15, and that these are subsequently cancelled.

The Agreement between the European Union and the Swiss Confederation on the linking of their greenhouse gas emissions trading systems of 23 November 2017 (‘Agreement’) provides for the mutual recognition of emission allowances that can be used for compliance under the Emissions Trading System of the European Union (‘EU ETS’) or the Emissions Trading System of Switzerland (‘ETS of Switzerland’). To operationalise the link between the EU ETS and the ETS of Switzerland, a direct link between the European Union Transaction Log (EUTL) of the Union Registry and the Swiss Supplementary Transaction Log (SSTL) of the Swiss registry will be established, which will enable the registry-to-registry transfer of emission allowances issued under either ETS (Article 3(2) of the Agreement). response:
The EU emissions trading system establishes a scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community to promote reductions of greenhouse gas emissions in a cost-effective and economically efficient manner [1]. 

Key operational elements include:
* **Allowances and Trading:** Any person may hold allowances [4], and allowances can be transferred between persons within the Community, as well as between persons within the Community and in third countries under specific conditions [3]. Member States must ensure registries are established and maintained for accurate accounting of the issue, holding, transfer, and cancellation of allowances [4]. 
* **Surrender of Allowances:** Operators of installations must surrender a number of allowances equal to their total verified emissions from the preceding calendar year [3][5]. 
* **Monitoring and Oversight:** ESMA regularly monitors the integrity and transparency of the European carbon market, including market volatility, price evolution, auctions, and trading operations [5].
* **Separate Sectors:** A separate but parallel emissions trading system is established for buildings, road transport, and additional sectors to avoid disturbing the system for stationary installations and aviation, supported by an efficient monitoring, reporting, and verification system [2].
reference: Allowances can be transferred between persons within the Union and with recognised third-country schemes. Each year the operator of each installation must surrender a number of allowances equal to its total verified emissions of the preceding year, and those allowances are then cancelled.

Based on the provided sources, specific emission limit values apply to various industrial installations, including waste incineration and co-incineration plants, combustion plants, and medium combustion plants:

* **Waste Incineration Plants:** Daily and half-hourly average emission limit values are set for substances such as total dust (10 mg/Nm³ daily; 30 or 10 mg/Nm³ half-hourly), TOC, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen fluoride, sulphur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$), and nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$) [1]. Heavy metals also have average emission limit values over a sampling period of 30 minutes to 8 hours (e.g., cadmium, thallium, and mercury at 0.05 mg/Nm³) [1].
* **Combustion Plants:** Specific emission limit values apply for $\text{SO}_2$ (e.g., general limit of 35 mg/Nm³ for gaseous fuels, 5 mg/Nm³ for liquefied gas) [2], $\text{NO}_x$ depending on fuel type, total rated thermal input, and plant characteristics [2][4][6], carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) [4][6], and dust (e.g., 5 mg/Nm³ in general for gaseous fuels, 20 mg/Nm³ for solid or liquid fuels with 50-300 MW input) [4]. Certain plants operating fewer than 1,500 hours per year are subject to specific $\text{NO}_x$ limits of 400 or 450 mg/Nm³ [2][6]. 
* **Medium Combustion Plants:** Annex II establishes specific emission limit values (including footnotes addressing specific sectors, plant sizes, fuels like biogas or heavy fuel oil, and operational hours such as for engines) [3][5].

user_input: What are the requirements for protecting natural habitats?
response:
Based on the provided sources, the requirements for protecting and conserving natural habitats include:

* **Conservation Measures and Management Plans:** Member States must establish necessary conservation measures for special areas of conservation, which may involve appropriate management plans specifically designed for the sites or integrated into other development plans, alongside statutory, administrative, or contractual measures matching the ecological requirements of Annex I natural habitats and Annex II species [1]. 
* **Prevention of Deterioration and Disturbance:** Member States must take appropriate steps in special areas of conservation to avoid the deterioration of natural habitats and species habitats, as well as significant disturbances of the species for which the areas were designated [1].
* **Assessment of Plans and Projects:** Any plan or project not directly connected with or necessary to the management of a site, but likely to have a significant effect thereon, must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site's conservation objectives [1]. Competent national authorities may only agree to the plan or project after ascertaining that it will not adversely affect the site's integrity [1].
* **Compensatory Measures and Public Interest:** If a plan or project must be carried out for imperative reasons of overriding public interest despite a negative assessment and a lack of alternatives, the Member State must take all necessary compensatory measures to ensure the overall coherence of Natura 2000 is protected and inform the Commission [1]. For priority natural habitat types or species, only considerations relating to human health, public safety, beneficial environmental consequences of primary importance, or Commission opinions on other overriding public interests may be raised [1].
* **Favourable Conservation Status:** Measures taken must be designed to maintain or restore natural habitats of Community interest at a favourable conservation status, taking account of economic, social, cultural requirements, and regional/local characteristics [2]. A natural habitat's conservation status is considered favourable when its natural range and areas covered are stable or increasing, its specific necessary structure and functions exist and are likely to continue, and the conservation status of its typical species is also favourable [3].
reference: For special areas of conservation, Member States must establish conservation measures, such as management plans, and avoid deterioration of habitats and significant disturbance of species. Any plan or project likely to have a significant effect on a site must undergo an appropriate assessment of its implications for the site's conservation objectives, and the authorities may only agree to it in the light of that assessment's conclusions.

user_input: What energy efficiency requirements apply to buildings?
response:
Based on Directive (EU) 2024/1275, the energy efficiency requirements applying to buildings include:

* **General minimum energy performance requirements** set by Member States to achieve at least cost-optimal levels (and more stringent reference values like nearly zero-energy building and zero-emission building requirements where relevant) [1][2]. These apply to new buildings, existing buildings undergoing major renovation, building elements forming part of the building envelope, and technical building systems [1].
* **Minimum energy performance standards** for existing buildings and building units, in accordance with Articles 3 and 9 [1]. For non-residential buildings, these standards ensure they do not exceed specified maximum energy performance thresholds (the 16% threshold from 2030, and the 26% threshold from 2033) [3].
* **Zero-emission building requirements** for new buildings, which apply from 1 January 2028 for new buildings owned by public bodies, and from 1 January 2030 for all new buildings [5]. Until those dates, new buildings must be at least nearly zero-energy buildings and meet minimum energy performance requirements [5].
* **Technical building system requirements** to optimise energy use, covering overall performance, installation, dimensioning, adjustment, control, and hydronic balancing [4].
* **Building element requirements** set for elements forming part of the building envelope when replaced or retrofitted, as well as system requirements for technical building systems when installed, replaced, or upgraded [1][2][4].
reference: Member States set minimum energy performance requirements at cost-optimal levels. New buildings must be zero-emission buildings from 1 January 2028 if owned by public bodies and from 1 January 2030 for all new buildings; until then they must be at least nearly zero-energy buildings.

user_input: How is the internal market for electricity organised?
response:
The internal market for electricity is organised under common rules established to create a truly integrated, competitive, consumer-centred, flexible, fair, and transparent market [1]. Its organisation and functioning are governed by several key principles and rules:

* **Market Rules and Principles:** Electricity markets must be operated such that prices are formed based on demand and supply [5], and market rules encourage free price formation while avoiding actions that prevent it [5]. Market participants enjoy objective, transparent, and non-discriminatory access to transmission and distribution networks [6]. Furthermore, market rules facilitate flexible generation, sustainable low-carbon generation, demand response, energy storage, and the decarbonisation of the electricity system [5][6].
* **Market Access and Operation:** Member States must ensure there are no undue barriers regarding market entry, operation, and exit within the internal market [2]. They must also guarantee a level playing field where electricity undertakings are subject to transparent, proportionate, and non-discriminatory rules, fees, and treatment (such as for balancing responsibility, wholesale market access, data access, switching, billing, and licensing) [2]. 
* **Day-Ahead and Intraday Markets:** Transmission system operators (TSOs) and Nominated Electricity Market Operators (NEMOs) jointly organise the management of integrated day-ahead and intraday markets to maximise trading efficiency and effectiveness [3]. These markets must be non-discriminatory, transparent, operationally secure while maximising transmission capacity use, and make no distinction between trades within a bidding zone and across bidding zones [3].
* **Cross-Border Trade and Cooperation:** Member States must ensure national law does not unduly hamper cross-border trade, consumer participation (including demand response), investments in variable/flexible generation, energy storage, electromobility, or new interconnectors [2]. Member States, regulatory authorities, and TSOs cooperate to foster a fully interconnected internal market that increases the integration of renewable energy sources, free competition, and supply security [1].
reference: Markets must be competitive, consumer-centred, flexible and non-discriminatory: national law must not hamper cross-border trade or consumer participation, prices must reflect actual demand and supply, and there must be no undue barriers and a level playing field. All customers are free to choose their supplier and have more than one contract, and suppliers are free to set their prices.

user_input: What ecodesign requirements apply to energy-related products?
response:
Under Directive 2009/125/EC, energy-related products covered by implementing measures must fulfill specific ecodesign requirements in order to be placed on the market and/or put into service [3]. 

More specifically, for air heating products, cooling products, fan coil units, and high temperature process chillers, the ecodesign requirements are set out in Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2016/2281 [1]. Compliance with these ecodesign requirements must be measured and calculated in accordance with the requirements set out in Annex III [1].

1. Where reference is made to this Article, passengers shall be offered free of charge:
(a) meals and refreshments in a reasonable relation to the waiting time;

(c) transport between the airport and place of accommodation (hotel or other).
2. In addition, passengers shall be offered free of charge two telephone calls, telex or fax messages, or e-mails.

response:
When a flight is cancelled, passengers have the following rights:

* **Assistance and Re-routing/Reimbursement:** Passengers must be offered assistance by the operating air carrier in accordance with Article 8 and Article 9(1)(a) and (2) [1]. This includes a choice between ticket reimbursement (or a return flight) and re-routing under comparable conditions, as well as meals, refreshments, and communication facilities [2][6]. If re-routing results in a departure at least the day after the planned departure, additional assistance with hotel accommodation and transport to/from the airport must also be provided [1].
* **Right to Compensation:** Passengers have the right to compensation in accordance with Article 7, unless they are informed of the cancellation within specific timeframes prior to departure (or if the cancellation is caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even with all reasonable measures) [1]. 
* **Information:** Passengers must be given an explanation concerning possible alternative transport when informed of the cancellation [1], and the operating air carrier must provide each affected passenger with a written notice setting out the rules for compensation and assistance, along with the contact details of the national designated body [4].
reference: The airline must offer assistance under Article 8 and care under Article 9, and compensation under Article 7 of EUR 250, 400 or 600 depending on flight distance. No compensation is due if passengers were told of the cancellation at least two weeks before departure, or later with an acceptable re-routing, or if the airline proves the cancellation was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken.
